lead: Command guidance keeps the guidance computer on the ground or launcher. A tracker watches target and missile, the computer works out a correction, and a radio or wire link sends it to the missile. Homing guidance moves the computer into the missile nose: a seeker looks at the target and steers without help from the launcher. Both exist because a ground computer can be large and cheap, while a missile seeker gives the final metres of accuracy when the link is jammed or the range is short.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.2 for the guidance-law taxonomy.

sections.h3: Command guidance: the loop stays outside

blocks.text: In command guidance the guidance computer stays on the ground, on a ship or in the launcher. A tracker—a radar or an optical sight—measures the target and the missile. The computer compares the two lines of sight and turns the difference into a steering command. An uplink carries that command to the missile, where a receiver moves the fins. The missile's position goes back to the tracker, so the loop closes outside the missile.

items: MCLOS, manual command to line of sight. The operator keeps a sight on the target and steers the missile with a joystick; the computer only passes the stick command to the fins. Cheap, but the operator must see both target and missile, and accuracy falls as range grows.

SACLOS, semi-automatic command to line of sight. The operator keeps the sight on the target only; the computer measures the missile's offset from the sight line and flies it back. Workload drops, so accuracy improves at longer range.

Beam riding. The launcher points a radar or laser beam at the target. The missile sits inside the beam and senses its own offset from the beam centre; the correction is generated on board or by the beam. The operator only holds the beam, but the beam must stay on the target until impact.

blocks.text: A radio uplink can be jammed; a wire link is hard to jam but limits range and lays a cable. Command guidance suits short-range anti-tank missiles and some surface-to-air missiles because the heavy computer stays on the ground.

sections.h3: Homing guidance: the seeker in the nose

blocks.text: Homing guidance puts a seeker in the missile nose. The seeker measures the direction of the target and its angular motion; the missile's own computer steers to null the line-of-sight rate, so the missile stays on a collision course. The three types differ in where the energy comes from.

items: Active. The missile carries both transmitter and receiver. It sends a radar pulse and listens for the echo. Fire-and-forget: the launcher can leave after launch. Cost and size are high, and the missile's small radar has short range.

Semi-active. The launcher illuminates the target; the missile carries only a receiver and homes on the reflected energy. The missile is cheaper and lighter than active, but the launcher must keep pointing at the target until impact.

Passive. The missile listens to energy the target itself emits—radar transmissions, infrared heat, or jamming signals (home-on-jam). It carries no transmitter and needs no illumination from the launcher. It works only against a target that emits, and flares or decoys can pull it away.

blocks.text: The trap is the name. Semi-active is not passive: a semi-active missile has a receiver and no transmitter, but the launcher still lights the target. Passive uses only the target's own radiation.

Range alone does not decide. A command link adds delay, so a fast crossing target needs a quick tracker and a quick operator. A homing seeker removes link delay but adds missile cost and size. Pick command guidance when the launcher can stay and the missile must be cheap. Pick homing when the final metres need the missile's own eye and the launcher must leave. A long-range missile often uses command or inertial mid-course and homing terminal. The table gives the trade in plain terms.

examples.question: A SACLOS system sees the missile 3 mrad off the line of sight at 2 km range. Closing speed is 800 m/s. Find the lateral offset and the acceleration the computer must command. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Convert the angle: 3 mrad = 0.003 rad. A milliradian is one-thousandth of a radian.
Lateral offset y = Rθ = 2000 m × 0.003 = 6 m. R is range and θ is the angle in radians.
Time to go t = R ÷ Vc = 2000 m ÷ 800 m/s = 2.5 s. Vc is closing speed.
For constant acceleration starting from zero lateral speed, y = ½at², so a = 2y ÷ t² = 2 × 6 m ÷ (2.5 s)² = 1.92 m/s².
examples.answer: The offset is 6 m and the commanded acceleration is 1.92 m/s², about 0.2 g.
examples.check:
range_m = 2000
theta_rad = 0.003
closing = 800
offset_m = range_m * theta_rad
t = range_m / closing
a = 2 * offset_m / t**2
g = 9.81
a_g = a / g
print(f'{offset_m:.1f}')
print(f'{t:.1f}')
print(f'{a:.2f}')
print(f'{a_g:.4f}')

traps: Semi-active is not passive. In semi-active the launcher illuminates the target; passive uses radiation the target emits itself.
MCLOS means the operator steers the missile. SACLOS means the operator only keeps the sight on the target and the computer steers.
Beam riding is command guidance, not homing, even when the receiver sits inside the missile. The missile follows an external beam.
Convert mrad to rad before multiplying by range: 3 mrad = 0.003 rad, not 3 rad.
Command guidance accuracy depends on tracking and link delay; a larger computer on the ground does not remove that delay.

quiz.q: State the three homing seeker types by their energy source.
quiz.a: Active: missile carries transmitter and receiver. Semi-active: missile carries a receiver and the launcher illuminates the target. Passive: missile listens to radiation the target emits.

quiz.q: Why does SACLOS reduce operator workload compared with MCLOS?
quiz.a: In MCLOS the operator must keep the sight on the target and also steer the missile by joystick. In SACLOS the operator only keeps the sight on the target; the computer measures the missile offset from the sight line and sends the steering command.

quiz.q: A tracker measures a 4 mrad error at 3 km range. Find the lateral offset in metres.
quiz.a: Convert 4 mrad = 0.004 rad. Offset y = Rθ = 3000 m × 0.004 = 12 m.

quiz.q: A student calls a semi-active missile passive. Correct the statement and explain the launcher's role.
quiz.a: Semi-active is not passive. A semi-active missile has a receiver and no transmitter, but the launcher illuminates the target and the missile homes on the reflection. A passive missile uses only energy emitted by the target and needs no launcher illumination.

quiz.q: Why can a wire-guided command missile resist radio jamming but still have limited range?
quiz.a: The steering command travels along a wire, not a radio link, so radio jamming does not break the command path. The wire spool and cable length limit range, and the operator must keep sight of the missile.

quiz.q: In command guidance, what does the uplink carry?
quiz.a: The uplink carries the steering command from the launcher computer to the missile receiver, which moves the fins.

quiz.q: Give one reason to use active homing and one cost penalty.
quiz.a: Active homing gives fire-and-forget: the launcher can leave after launch because the missile carries its own transmitter and receiver. The penalty is higher missile cost and size, and the small seeker has shorter range than a large launcher radar.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern missiles mix command and homing: a radio datalink gives mid-course updates, then an active or passive seeker takes over for the last few kilometres. Fibre-optic guided missiles extend the wire idea with a video link. Search for dual-mode seeker, command to line of sight, and missile datalink to go further.
